title: How Long Can We Last
primary_metric: months of essential-expense coverage a given emergency-fund size actually provides, tested against the household's documented 7-month worst realistic income stretch

options.A: The Rule-of-Thumb Fund — a flat 3 months of the household's total essential expenses ($17,622), stop adding once reached and invest everything beyond it starting now
options.B: The Real-Stretch Fund — sized to cover the household's actual monthly shortfall (essential expenses minus Renata's guaranteed income alone) for the full 7-month dry spell documented in the household's own income records ($20,237), keep saving until reached before investing anything beyond it

deliverables.text: An essential-expense percent breakdown: using Appendix A's dollar figures, calculate what percent of the household's total monthly essential expenses each category represents, and identify the single largest category.

Julian's typical monthly freelance income, derived (not looked up): using Appendix B's slow-month invoice total and its stated percent of a typical month, calculate Julian's typical monthly freelance income.

The dollar size of both fund options, each calculated with a proportion (dollars of coverage per month, scaled to the number of months required): the Rule-of-Thumb Fund (Option A) and the Real-Stretch Fund (Option B).

A survival test for each fund: using a proportion, calculate exactly how many months of coverage each fund size provides against the household's documented monthly shortfall during the dry spell, and what percent of the full dry spell that represents, with a final recommendation.

appendices.title: The Osei Household's Essential Monthly Expenses
The Dry Spell, and How Each Fund Is Calculated

balance.argument_a: The Rule-of-Thumb Fund needs $17,622 (3 x the household's $5,874 in monthly essential expenses) -- $2,615 less than Option B, a real and immediately usable amount of capital the household can start investing today instead of continuing to save. It is also the single most widely cited emergency-fund benchmark in consumer personal finance (see Appendix E), meaning Renata and Julian do not need to defend an unusual number to anyone who asks how they picked it, and the household reaches it roughly a month sooner than Option B at their documented $709/month savings rate.
balance.argument_b: Tested against the household's own documented worst dry spell -- 7 straight months of $0 freelance income, with Renata's income unchanged -- the Rule-of-Thumb Fund runs out after covering only about 6.1 of the 7 months (87% of the stretch), leaving the household to cover the final $2,615 of essential expenses with credit-card debt or an asset sale, precisely the outcome an emergency fund exists to prevent. The Real-Stretch Fund, at $20,237, covers the documented stretch in full, for a cost of only 14.8% more saved -- a real, computed premium, not a vague 'better safe than sorry.'
balance.margin_basis: Fund_A = 3 x essential_monthly_expenses = 3 x $5,874 = $17,622. Fund_B = documented_dry_spell_months x monthly_shortfall, where monthly_shortfall = essential_monthly_expenses - Renata's_income = $5,874 - $2,983 = $2,891/month (Julian's income is $0 throughout the documented dry spell, per Appendix C/MA2), so Fund_B = 7 x $2,891 = $20,237. Fund_A's actual coverage against the $2,891/month shortfall is $17,622 / $2,891 = 6.10 months, i.e. 87.1% of the 7-month documented stretch -- it runs dry with about 0.9 months (roughly 27 days) of the stretch still remaining. margin_pct = (Fund_B - Fund_A) / Fund_A x 100 = ($20,237 - $17,622) / $17,622 x 100 = 14.84%, comfortably inside the SPEC §2 20% cap and within the case's 10-15% target range.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Julian's slow-month invoice total ($756), as a percent of his typical month
modeling_assumptions.basis: This case's own household record (Appendix B), chosen to give Challenge 3's D2 a clean, calculable relationship ($756 / 0.21 = $3,600). No public dataset publishes a 'percent of typical month' figure for an individual freelancer's worst month specifically. The general magnitude (a swing near 21%) is informed by JPMorgan Chase Institute's finding [S4] that the vast majority of young, bottom-income-quintile, or Western workers experience month-to-month total-income swings exceeding 30% -- establishing that a swing in this broad range is a realistic magnitude for a volatile earner, though this case's specific 21% figure and its 'percent of typical' framing (rather than JPMC's 'swing size') are this case's own chosen value, not a direct citation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changing this percent changes only the derived value of Julian's typical monthly income in D2 (a standalone percent exercise). It does not appear anywhere else in the case and plays no role in sizing either fund (D3/D4), which depend only on essential expenses, Renata's income, and MA2's dry-spell length.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Length and severity of Julian's documented worst freelance dry spell
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public dataset reports an exact consecutive-month 'income fully stops' duration for freelance workers generally. Informed by two real, directly-verified findings: the Federal Reserve's 2024 household survey [S3], which found 56% of self-employed adults (excluding gig-platform work) report income varies month to month vs. 26% of people who work for someone else -- establishing this kind of variability as a persistent pattern, not a one-off; and JPMorgan Chase Institute's 2018 Online Platform Economy report [S5], which found 58% of transportation (rideshare-style) platform earners had their platform earnings concentrated in three or fewer months of the year -- directional support that many non-salaried earners go multiple consecutive months with little or no income from a given income source. Neither source reports this exact length-and-severity combination for a project-based freelance consultant specifically; the specific 7-month, $0 scenario is this case's own stated choice, disclosed rather than presented as a direct citation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single assumption most likely to change which option wins. Flexing the dry-spell length (holding severity at total stoppage) directly rescales Fund B and therefore margin_pct; see sensitivity_model.py for the exact flex range that keeps Option B's recommendation defensible without breaching the SPEC §2 20% cap.

sensitivity_note: This case touches a real personal-finance stressor for irregular-income households (freelance/1099 income insecurity) -- a one-line facilitator flag per SPEC §6 for the discussion lead. Stakes are real but comparably modest (a savings/investing timing decision for an employed, dual-income household), not illness, death, or acute hardship.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The exact length of Julian's NEXT freelance dry spell is a forecast/irreducible unknown -- no amount of research can establish in advance how long a future income interruption will last for this specific household. The case fixes 7 months as this household's own documented worst historical stretch (case.md Appendix C), informed by real supporting data (Federal Reserve SHED 2024: 56% of self-employed adults report month-to-month income variability as a persistent pattern, source S3; JPMorgan Chase Institute 2018 report: 58% of transportation-platform earners had platform earnings concentrated in 3 or fewer months of the year, source S5), but is disclosed as a stated Modeling Assumption (MA2) rather than a directly-cited figure, since neither source reports this exact length/severity combination. Tier 2 P5 flexing +/-50% confirms the base-case verdict (Option B wins by 14.84%) is genuinely sensitive to this value: at -50% (3.5 months) the verdict flips to Option A (Fund A already covers 174% of a shorter stretch); at +50% (10.5 months) the margin widens past the SPEC section 2 20% cap to 72.3%. This instability is surfaced explicitly in FACILITATOR.md Anchor 4 so a facilitator never defends the 14.84% margin as unconditionally true -- it holds specifically at this household's documented 7-month history, not as a general claim about freelance income volatility.
